title: Peter Thiel: The AI Crisis, Europe’s Decline & the Battle for America
subtitle: AI progress, stagnation risks, and European technology strategy
description: Peter Thiel and Mathias Döpfner discuss whether AI can restart broad growth, the risks of stagnation and global slowdown proposals, and Europe's ability to build and scale technology companies. Thiel's political judgments, analogies, and forecasts are attributed arguments, not established causal findings; his Palantir adoption example is a first-party account.
source: MDMEETS - Essential Talks with Mathias Döpfner

title: A Cheeky Pint with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei
subtitle: AI product adoption, model economics, and review interfaces
description: Dario Amodei and John Collison discuss why coding tools are adopted faster than other AI applications, how overlapping model generations affect company economics, and why agent products need manageable review interfaces. The profitability example is hypothetical, not audited company results. Customer outcomes are first-party claims, timelines are forecasts, and the product strategy is Amodei's advocacy.

title: The Adolescence of Technology
subtitle: A five-part framework for risks from powerful AI
description: Dario Amodei separates risks from autonomous model behavior, destructive misuse, deliberate power concentration, economic disruption, and indirect effects, then proposes technical and policy responses. Anthropic's CEO assumes powerful AI and offers his own risk framework and policy proposals, not a complete list of risks or a consensus view.

title: Machines of Loving Grace
subtitle: How intelligence interacts with real-world bottlenecks
description: Dario Amodei explores a favorable future with powerful AI: which work could accelerate, and where experiments, missing evidence, institutions, adoption, or physical limits would still constrain progress. Its sector outcomes and timelines are speculative first-party forecasts conditional on the assumed arrival of powerful AI.

title: Dario Amodei: Anthropic CEO on Claude, AGI & the Future of AI & Humanity
subtitle: Scaling, model steering, computer use, prompting, and mechanistic interpretability
description: Lex Fridman interviews Anthropic's Dario Amodei on scaling, computer use, and safety; Amanda Askell on prompting and constitutional AI; and Chris Olah on how neural networks compute. The episode combines technical explanations with Anthropic leaders' first-party accounts and dated forecasts; it is not an independent evaluation of Claude's capabilities or safety.

title: AI and eCommerce with Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke
subtitle: Shopper-agent simulation, outcome signals, and human–AI evaluation
description: Tobi Lütke, Richard Sutton, Sendhil Mullainathan, and fellow panelists examine Shopify's SimGym shopper agents, which navigate stores through a vision-model browser loop. They distinguish interface operation, predictive validity, real commercial outcomes, and benchmarks for people working with AI. Product accuracy and benefits are participant accounts, not independent evaluations.

title: Il rischio AI è ormai accettato
subtitle: Salvatore Sanfilippo on AI risk, cautious progress, and model-size limits
description: Salvatore Sanfilippo distinguishes acknowledging AI risk from predicting imminent extinction. He discusses cyber and biological misuse, recursive self-improvement, and international coordination, then proposes limits on model parameter counts rather than a complete research stop. Italian-language opinion commentary; his risk assessments and proposed safeguards are not validated safety findings.

title: Sir Demis Hassabis on the AI Revolution, the Future of AI and Human Creativity | Hannah Fry
subtitle: RSA Albert Medal conversation on AI and human creativity
description: Demis Hassabis and Hannah Fry discuss AI-assisted creative prototyping, why human experience may still matter in art, and who shapes the benefits of more autonomous AI. Hassabis proposes personalized tutoring alongside collaborative classrooms and argues for valuing health and inspiration in architecture. His optimistic forecasts and first-party accounts are presented as views, not independently established outcomes.

title: The next 50 years: humanity, AI, power | Yuval Noah Harari
subtitle: Language, economic power, and human agency
description: Yuval Noah Harari and Tom Parker discuss how AI could gain power through economic and legal systems. Harari connects that forecast to democratic conversation, technological dependence, intimate relationships, and the difference between solving problems and choosing worthwhile goals.

title: AI has hacked the code of human civilization | Yuval Noah Harari
subtitle: AI agency, bureaucracy, and language-based institutions
description: In his 2026 Tanner Lecture, Yuval Noah Harari argues that AI could gain influence by operating the language-based institutions through which people already coordinate society. His examples connect bureaucratic authority to finance, news selection, and intimate relationships; the title's hacking metaphor is not a software exploit.

title: Yuval Noah Harari on Donald Trump’s Core Delusion | The Ezra Klein Show
subtitle: Cooperation, political narratives, and AI's influence on intimacy and accountability
description: Ezra Klein and Yuval Noah Harari discuss cooperation, liberal institutions, Israel and Palestine, then algorithmic media, AI relationships, and accountability. The first hour is primarily politics and history; their later AI debate weighs personalized assistance against proposed risks of manipulation and loss of human control.

title: Building Trust in the Age of Disinformation – What Future Awaits Us? | Yuval Noah Harari
subtitle: Algorithmic trust, European AI dependence, and language-based authority
description: Yuval Noah Harari and Marijana Grbeša discuss how algorithms mediate trust, Europe's AI dependence, and the distinction between language-based intelligence and human experience. Harari forecasts changes to financial and religious authority; closing passages address war rather than AI.

title: AI's Hidden Debt Problem Explained
subtitle: Hyperscaler spending commitments, future leases, and financial guarantees
description: The Plain Bagel distinguishes purchase commitments, project funding, future leases, and financial guarantees in AI infrastructure spending. His analysis explains why headline totals are not equivalent to ordinary debt while arguing that fixed payments reduce flexibility if AI demand disappoints.

title: AI's mathematical results are not a bad thing
subtitle: Salvatore Sanfilippo on AI-generated proofs, human expertise, and learning from machine results
description: Salvatore Sanfilippo argues that AI-generated mathematical proofs can add knowledge and become material for human study, simplification, and new techniques. He connects reactions to these results with the loss of professional status felt when coding agents outperform familiar work. His account of the result and Terence Tao's position is opinion commentary, not an independent mathematical assessment.

title: Paul Graham On Startups, Ambition, and Great Founders
subtitle: Founder motivation, milestone funding, and why AI does not remove the need to ship
description: Paul Graham discusses ambition, founder determination, starting with limited capital, and YC's batch model. The AI-relevant sections cover uneven model capabilities, shipping speed as a continuing signal, and inference bills as a new startup cost. A founder interview offering experience and opinion, not a coding-agent tutorial or a measured forecast of AI economics.

title: Sam Altman on Astra, AGI, and the future of OpenAI
subtitle: Frontier training safety, computer-use agents, and the convergence of chat and coding
description: Sam Altman discusses delayed frontier reinforcement-learning runs, alignment as following user intent, Astra computer use, and a unified ChatGPT/Codex experience. He also addresses compute constraints, privacy, and OpenAI's product priorities. A company leader's account and roadmap, not an independent evaluation of model capabilities or safety guarantees.

title: Sam Altman on Building OpenAI & Betting on the Impossible
subtitle: Hands-on adoption, context-rich agents, iterative deployment, and research feedback loops
description: David Senra asks Sam Altman how AI adoption, context, product strategy, and research management shape OpenAI. Altman points to Tobi Lütke’s hands-on agent use, admits that habits and product gaps slow adoption, argues for iterative deployment and accident reporting, and proposes context-rich persistent agents. His capability, safety, and market claims are first-party reports or forecasts, and the privacy implications of broad context access go unaddressed.

title: Why AI Models Stop Learning — Rich Sutton and Khurram Javed
subtitle: Continual learning, the Big World Hypothesis, and a research path beyond frozen model weights
description: Rich Sutton and Khurram Javed argue that deployed LLMs stay static because their weights do not update from experience. They propose continual learning from the real world, per-weight step-size optimization, Continual Backprop, and self-discovered abstractions as a path toward agents that keep adapting. Their claims about synthetic data, forgetting, and replacing the current LLM paradigm describe Oak Lab’s research agenda, not a system demonstrated at frontier scale.

title: AI concepts — Salvatore Sanfilippo
description: An Italian-language research notebook on model representations, reasoning, interpretability, architecture claims, open weights, local inference, efficiency, and speculative questions about AI and cosmology. The guided summary frames the playlist as conceptual grounding for evaluating coding agents rather than as a settled theory of AI.
